papers.title_in_file: Rethinking Noise in Quantum Machine Learning: When Noise Improves Learning
papers.what_it_is: A numerical study of how an effective (phenomenological) noise model changes the accuracy of 55 differently initialized quantum graph neural networks predicting the QM9 HOMO-LUMO gap.

assertions.value: The authors report that, among 55 independently initialized QGNN models on the QM9 HOMO-LUMO gap task, 36.4% gained more than 2% in R2 when the effective noise was added, 14.5% lost more than 2%, and 49.1% changed only marginally.
assertions.anchor: Section III Results, Fig. 2(b) caption, p.3-4
quotes: We examined the effect of quantum noise on single-layer QGNN performance using a systematic study of 55 independently initialized models trained on the QM9 HOMO-LUMO gap prediction task.
Distribution of performance changes, revealing 36.4% beneficial (> 2%), 14.5% detrimental
The remaining 49.1% exhibited marginal responses within
assertions.certainty_reason: One empirical study with one architecture, one dataset and one effective noise model.
assertions.reader_inference: The noise is a phenomenological output-level model, not simulated gate channels, so the split does not describe real hardware noise.

assertions.value: The authors report a strong negative correlation between baseline model performance and noise benefit, and they read it as a regularization-like effect for under-optimized models.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Section III, Fig. 2(d), p.1 and p.4
quotes: We identify a strong negative correlation
Figure 2(d) reveals a clear negative correlation between
assertions.certainty_reason: Correlation over 55 runs of one setup; the regularization reading is an interpretation.
assertions.reader_inference: The correlation coefficient is printed in the paper (abstract and Fig. 2(d)); this entry keeps it out of the value because the minus sign does not copy as plain text. Selecting each model's best noise level among four profiles and then reporting the gain can inflate the benefit.

assertions.value: The authors state that the results do not by themselves establish that the improvement is unique to physical quantum noise, and that the study covers single-layer QGNNs on molecular property prediction under a phenomenological noise model.
assertions.anchor: Section III (end) and Section IV Conclusion, p.5-6
quotes: We also note that the present results do not by themselves establish that the observed improvement is unique to physical quantum noise.
This study examines single-layer QGNNs on molecular property prediction as a foundational case for understanding quantum noise effects.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state their own scope and limit in Section III and Section IV, p.5-6.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper cannot separate quantum-specific noise effects from generic stochastic regularization.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Autoencoder: An efficient approach to quantum feature map generation
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, related work, results discussion and conclusion. The sample-complexity theory section was not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A simulated study that pre-trains quantum autoencoders on 3 million peptide sequences and uses the learned states as quantum-kernel SVM features on seven peptide classification datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report that quantum autoencoder representations gave accuracy improvements of 0.4% to 8.1% over Hamiltonian-evolution baselines across seven peptide datasets, with an average gain of +2.9%.
quotes: Results show that quantum autoencoder learned representations achieve accuracy improvements ranging from 0.4% to 8.1% over Hamiltonian baselines across seven datasets
the quantum autoencoder improved classification accuracy across all datasets, with an average gain of +2.9%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; best variant picked per dataset by cross-validation.
assertions.reader_inference: The comparison is against one fixed quantum encoding, not against a classical model, so it says nothing about advantage over classical methods.

assertions.value: The authors state that their objective is not to demonstrate quantum advantage over classical approaches, and that they do not compare the quantum autoencoder directly against protein language models or other classical methods.
quotes: In this work, our primary objective is not to demonstrate quantum advantage over classical approaches
We do not compare quantum autoencoders directly against PLMs or other classical methods
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of scope, Section 1, p.2-3.

assertions.value: The authors state that all experiments were run on simulators without device noise and that the quantum evaluations were restricted to kernel-based SVMs.
quotes: all experiments were conducted on simulators without device noise.
quantum evaluations were restricted to kernel-based SVMs.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limitation in the Section 4 discussion, p.13.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum Machine Learning via Contrastive Training
papers.what_it_is: A trapped-ion demonstration of self-supervised contrastive pretraining of a four-qubit encoder on small binary images, followed by fine-tuned classification compared with random initialization.

assertions.value: The authors report that fine-tuning a contrastively pretrained encoder gave higher mean test accuracy and lower variability than random initialization at every labeled-data budget tested, with the main statistics from noiseless simulation and a few points checked on the trapped-ion processor.
assertions.anchor: Section 3 Results, Fig. 4, p.9-10; Abstract p.1
quotes: Across all labeled training data budgets, the model assisted by a contrastively trained encoder provides both higher mean accuracy and lower variability than a network trained from random initialization.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result on a toy dataset from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The distribution statistics come from simulation; the hardware shows one data draw per budget, so hardware variance is not measured.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experiment used four qubits of a seven-ion trapped-ion computer, on a target set of 28 Bars-and-Stripes images and 253 diagonal images.
assertions.anchor: Section 2 Setup p.3; Section 3 Results p.9
quotes: We conduct the experiment using four qubits selected from a seven-ion programmable trapped-ion quantum computer
The target image classes contain 28 BAS images and a total of 253 diagonal images.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own description of its setup, Section 2 and Section 3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the absolute accuracy is limited by the protocol choices, and that a single dataset is used to evaluate both models on the quantum processor.
assertions.anchor: Section 3 Fig. 4 caption p.10; Section 4 Discussion p.11
quotes: A single dataset is used to evaluate both models on the quantum processor.
The absolute accuracy in this demonstration is limited by the protocol choices
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limits in the Fig. 4 caption and the Discussion.

papers.title_in_file: On quantum backpropagation, information reuse, and cheating measurement collapse
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, Definition 1, Section 3 start, Theorem 9 statement, Section 6 discussion and the Appendix C single-copy argument. Proofs were not read in full.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper on whether parameterized quantum models can compute gradients at a cost comparable to classical backpropagation, with and without access to multiple copies of a state.

assertions.value: The authors state that achieving backpropagation scaling is impossible without access to multiple copies of a state, and in the single-copy appendix they argue that no efficient procedure can exist in the most general case unless pseudo-random quantum states can be efficiently cloned.
quotes: We show that achieving backpropagation scaling is impossible without access to multiple copies of a state.
Here we argue that no efficient procedure can exist in the most general case, unless it is possible to efficiently clone pseudo-random quantum states.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states it as shown, but Appendix C says information-theoretic bounds do not rule it out and gives a computational argument under a cryptographic assumption.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract wording is stronger than the appendix. The appendix says the single-copy task is information-theoretically viable (Proposition 16) and rules it out only computationally.

assertions.value: The authors state that with access to multiple copies of a state, they give an algorithm based on shadow tomography that matches backpropagation scaling in quantum resources, while the classical auxiliary cost is left tied to open problems in shadow tomography.
quotes: With this added ability, we introduce an algorithm with foundations in shadow tomography that matches backpropagation scaling in quantum resources while reducing classical auxiliary computational costs to open problems in shadow tomography.
assertions.certainty_reason: Theorem 9 (quantum-efficient backpropagation), p.6; proofs in Appendix D.

assertions.value: The authors state that their proposal requires classical storage and manipulation of a hypothesis state, which gives an exponential classical overhead unless an approximation scheme can be applied.
quotes: Our proposal, however, houses a large caveat: it requires the classical storage and manipulation of a hypothesis state, which results in an exponential classical overhead, unless an approximation scheme can be effectively applied.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' stated caveat, Section 1, p.3.

papers.title_in_file: Reservoir Computing Using Measurement-Controlled Quantum Dynamics
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, results (classification and Mackey-Glass forecasting), discussion and conclusions. The atom-cavity derivation in Sections 2 and 3 was skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A proposal and numerical validation of a quantum reservoir computer built on the measurement-controlled dynamics of a probed atom in a cavity.

assertions.value: The authors report that their reservoir with 16 neurons reached 99.7% accuracy on the sinusoidal-square waveform classification task, and that the reservoir with 8 neurons reached approximately 90%.
quotes: Notably, the reservoir with just 8 neurons demonstrates an accuracy of approximately 90% and RMSE of approximately 0.1.
increasing the number of neurons to 16 results in a significant improvement, yielding a remarkable 99.7% accuracy and a reduced error of 4
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one numerical study.

assertions.value: The authors report that, using code from a cited reference, a traditional reservoir produced a free-running MGTS forecast of comparable accuracy only with more than 500 neurons, while their quantum reservoir used 16 neurons.
quotes: Using the computer code from Ref. [21] we established that a traditional RC system can produce a free-running forecast of comparable accuracy only when the reservoir contains more than 500 neurons
The reservoir has 16 neurons and it was trained on
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own comparison in one study; the classical baseline was run with the authors' chosen hyperparameters.
assertions.reader_inference: Neuron counts of different reservoir types are not a like-for-like cost measure, and the quantum reservoir was simulated classically.

assertions.value: The authors state that the proposed atom-in-cavity quantum reservoir is validated theoretically.
quotes: We theoretically validate the operation of the reservoir, demonstrating its potential to be used in error-tolerant applications
we propose and theoretically validate a novel quantum RC architecture that exploits the dynamics of an atom trapped in a cavity.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of how the reservoir is validated, Abstract and Section 1.
assertions.reader_inference: No hardware experiment is reported; the evidence is numerical.

papers.title_in_file: Experimental investigation of single qubit quantum classifier with small number of samples
papers.what_it_is: A silicon-photonic single-qubit data re-uploading classifier trained with very few photons per input, with simulations and chip experiments.

assertions.value: The authors report a classification accuracy of 86.1% on the photonic chip when trained with an average of 1.6 photon samples per input and 200 training points.
quotes: classifier trained with an average sample number of M = 1.6 and 200 training data points
the final classification accuracy reached an impressive 86.1%.
assertions.certainty_reason: One experimental run on one task.

assertions.value: The authors report that with the average number of photon samples per input reduced to approximately two, the classifier achieved nearly 90% accuracy, provided the training dataset was sufficiently large.
quotes: Even when the average number of photon samples per input was reduced to approximately two, the classifier achieved nearly 90% accuracy, provided that the training dataset was sufficiently large.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study on one task.
assertions.reader_inference: The only experimental figure in the body text at this photon level is 86.1%; the conclusion says accuracies exceeding 90% while the abstract says nearly 90%, so the exact value is read off Fig. 4(b).

assertions.value: The authors state that the classifier is a three-layer data re-uploading model, and that the task is a single circular decision boundary in two dimensions.
assertions.anchor: Section III p.3; Section IV p.4
quotes: The classifier implemented a three-layer Data Reuploading model, with each layer applying a unitary transformation controlled by data-encoded phase shifts.
The classification task involved a circular decision boundary centered at
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's description of its own model and task, Sections III and IV.

assertions.value: The authors state that they observed a noticeable drop in accuracy when the photon sample number M dropped below 10, and that whether more training data can overcome this is an open question.
assertions.anchor: Section III end, p.4; Section V p.5
quotes: Additionally, we observed a noticeable drop in accuracy when M dropped below 10.
Whether this degradation can be overcome by further increasing the training dataset remains an open question for future work.

papers.title_in_file: Adiabatic training for Variational Quantum Algorithms
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, introduction, model description start, results tables and analysis, and conclusions. The QUBO derivation was skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: A simulated hybrid scheme that trains a quantum recurrent neural network for stock-price trend prediction by casting parameter search as a QUBO solved with an annealing simulator.

assertions.value: The authors report that the accuracy of the QRNN with adiabatic training is similar to the QRNN with classical gradient-descent training, with a slight positive difference when more than 200 training records were used.
assertions.anchor: Section 6 Results analysis, Table 4, p.10; Section 7 Conclusions, p.10
quotes: Our results show that the accuracy of QRNN with adiabatic training is similar to QRNN with classical gradient-descend training.
there is a slight positive difference with respect to classical training when the volume of data used for training is greater than 200 records.
assertions.certainty_reason: Small simulated experiment on a few stock series; accuracies in Table 4 differ by a few points either way.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 4 shows adiabatic training below classical training on two of the five series, so the wording slight positive difference holds only for the larger sets.

assertions.value: The authors state that for adiabatic training the execution count is constant and the time required is substantially smaller for a fixed number of binary variables.
quotes: However, for adiabatic training, the EC is constant and the time required is substantially smaller for a fixed number of binary variables (see Table 6).
assertions.certainty_reason: Timing from software simulators in one study.
assertions.reader_inference: The times are for a quantum annealing simulator on a personal computer, so they say nothing about annealing hardware time.

assertions.value: The authors state that the gate-based and annealing models were simulated with software libraries, and that validation on real noisy hardware is left to further research.
quotes: both gate-based and annealing quantum models were simulated using the corresponding software libraries from IBM-Qiskit and D-Wave Ocean
Validation of the obtained results against executions on real noisy hardware will be subject of further research.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of scope, Section 5, p.9.

assertions.value: The authors state that the binary nature of QUBO models makes the variational algorithm lose expressiveness because the rotation angles are discretized.
quotes: the binary nature of the QUBO models makes the Variational Algorithms lose expressiveness because of the discretization of the rotation angles.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit in the Conclusions, p.11.

papers.title_in_file: Portfolio construction using a sampling-based variational quantum scheme
papers.what_it_is: An IBM and Vanguard study that runs a sampling-based CVaR variational algorithm with local-search postprocessing on a simplified bond-ETF portfolio problem, up to 109 qubits on IBM Heron hardware.

assertions.value: The authors report utility-scale experiments on IBM Heron processors with 109 qubits and up to 4200 gates, and a best post-local-search optimization gap of 0.49% (TwoLocal bilinear), followed by 0.55% (TwoLocal color) and 0.91% (BFCD color).
assertions.anchor: Abstract p.1; Section IV results, p.6
quotes: Our utility-scale experiments on IBM Heron processors involve 109 qubits and up to 4200 gates, achieving a relative solution error of 0.49%.
The best performance after local search is achieved by the TwoLocal bilinear ansatz (0.49% optimization gap), followed by the TwoLocal color (0.55%) and BFCD color (0.91%).
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one problem instance.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results provide evidence that a combined quantum-classical workflow can bring samples close to the optimal, which cannot be achieved by only using the local search method.
assertions.anchor: Section V Conclusions, p.7; Section I p.2
quotes: Our results provide evidence that a combined quantum-classical workflow can bring samples close to the optimal, which is something that cannot be achieved by only using the local search method.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' reading of one instance; they call it evidence, not proof.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors also report that the BFCD circuit post-processed result resembles the post-processed initial distribution, so the benefit depends on the circuit.

assertions.value: The authors state that the simplified problem with 109 bonds can be solved to optimality by classical solvers like CPLEX or Gurobi in a few seconds.
quotes: The simplified problem with 109 bonds, on the other hand, can be solved by classical solvers like CPLEX or Gurobi to optimality in a few seconds
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of the instance scope, Section II, p.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that little can be inferred about runtime at large scale from experiments of small to mid problem size, and that an advantage over classical methods requires scaling to a regime where classical solvers struggle.
quotes: we believe that little can be inferred about the runtime at large scale, from experiments of small to mid problem size, given the heuristic nature of the methods.
it is essential to scale the problem size to a much larger regime, where classical solvers struggle.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit in Section V, p.7.
